blocks.text: Takeaway: One chain, three layers — upstream supplies chips and core components, midstream turns parts into systems and buildings into powered data halls, downstream operates capacity and sells to the applications that pay for the whole chain. The binding constraints are power and electrical equipment (structural: OEMs won't or can't expand); memory and packaging are tight but expanding; cooling and optics self-correct. Credit lives downstream and on the power side — colo, hyperscaler SPVs, neoclouds, power generation and software ARR — while upstream is equity territory. Cost of capital is compressing fast: CoreWeave moved from private credit to HY to an A3-rated facility in ~2 years, and the Meta-vs-Hyperion gap shows a ~150bp structural premium still available to private credit on the same underlying credit (Junson calculation). Under-appreciated angles: ODM inventory/receivables ABF; power-side project finance; sponsor direct lending behind PE roll-ups of electrical-equipment and cooling niche champions.

blocks.html: 1. Value Chain: three layers, from chips to the end-user
blocks.text: 1. Value Chain: three layers, from chips to the end-user

blocks.html: Upstream supplies the five components carrying the bulk of AI server BOM value: GPU, HBM, advanced packaging (CoWoS), PCB/substrate, optical modules. Midstream runs two production lines — components into complete racks, shells into powered halls — with power generation increasingly procured directly behind both (“power is the new land”). Downstream has its own structure: colo is the landlord layer (Equinix, Digital Realty, Vantage, GDS); hyperscalers span two layers — own data centers, plus largest tenant of colo and largest buyer of neocloud capacity; neoclouds are compute sub-landlords (CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe); AI labs are the demand layer; software & data platforms ride total volume as a horizontal service layer without single-name risk; end applications ultimately pay for the chain.

blocks.html: 2. Supply Bottlenecks: power and electrical equipment are the hard constraints
blocks.text: 2. Supply Bottlenecks: power and electrical equipment are the hard constraints

blocks.html: The binding constraint has migrated down the physical stack — GPUs (2023) → HBM & packaging (2024–25) → power & electrical equipment (now) — each on a longer replacement cycle. Downstream delays are transmitted, not home-grown: 30–50% of US capacity planned for 2026 is expected to be delayed or cancelled (Bloomberg citing Sightline Climate, May-26). For underwriting, construction delay is now the base case: the first diligence question on a development loan has shifted from “is the lease signed” to “are the transformer and turbine slots locked”.

Self-correcting bottlenecks with 6–12-month expansion cycles (industry convention) — “expensive but available”

blocks.html: Won't vs can't: turbine OEMs won't expand — scarred by the mid-2010s bust, they cannot verify how much of the book is double-ordering, so they stretch lead times, raise prices and demand 6–8-yr reservations with deposits; supply discipline is itself the most honest read on demand quality. Transformer makers largely can't — GOES concentration, hand-winding workforce retiring, scarce test bays. Whether today's queues end in continued shortage or a post-2028 glut is the key swing factor.

blocks.html: 3. Equity or Credit? Two questions decide the instrument
blocks.text: 3. Equity or Credit? Two questions decide the instrument

blocks.html: Credit asks ① what repays the loan (cash-flow contractedness) and ② what can be seized if it isn't (collateral). Two credit bands emerge: an asset-backed band (colo 10–15-yr leases; hyperscaler SPVs; power PPAs of 10–20 yrs; ABS / project bonds / ABF) and a cash-flow band (direct lending against software ARR, NRR >100%). Only two segments clear 8%+ cash yield: neoclouds and software ARR. Upstream (fabless chips, optics, labs, apps) answers neither question — equity-only. The axes gate credit, not equity: top-right equity earns development spreads and contracted rent (infrastructure-style); bottom-left earns growth and multiple expansion (venture-style). Within neocloud lending, collateral tiers rank: contract pledge > building + lease > pure GPU residual — GPUs lose roughly half their value within 2–3 years, which is both the premise and the risk of GPU financing.

blocks.html: 4. Capital Market Depth: where each instrument is deep
blocks.text: 4. Capital Market Depth: where each instrument is deep

items: Upstream: public equity + IG bonds only; private credit penetration ≈0 (fabless leaves nothing to seize; cash cows don't borrow expensive money). Chipmakers are turning reverse financiers — NVIDIA up to $2bn in xAI's GPU SPV (Bloomberg, Oct-25), $2bn each to Nebius and CoreWeave (Nebius 6-K / TheNextWeb, Mar-26) — the circular-financing debate is a live test of end-demand.

Midstream: the only deep PE cell in the chain — transformer / switchgear / cooling niche champions (marquee deal: KKR–CoolIT (KKR, 2023)) with sponsor DL following; ODM GPU-inventory and receivables ABF is the cell most likely to deepen next.
Colo: the only full-capital-structure row — development loans → ABS ($27bn issued in 2025 (KBRA, Mar-26); Vantage ~$7.5bn across 9 deals (CNBC; TechRepublic, Jun-25)) → mezz / HoldCo → IG.

Hyperscaler, two tracks: on-balance-sheet IG (Meta $30bn, $125bn book, 10Y +78bp (S&P via FI Desk, Oct-25)) vs off-balance-sheet SPV (Hyperion $27.3bn, Blue Owl 80%, S&P A+, ~UST+225bp, PIMCO anchor (IFR; WSJ / Bloomberg, Oct-25)) — same underlying credit, ~150bp structural premium to private credit (Junson calculation).

Neocloud cost-of-capital ladder in ~2 years: $7.5bn private credit, Blackstone-led (CoreWeave, May-24) → HY 8.50–9.75% + converts (CoreWeave 8-K, Sep-26) → $8.5bn A3-rated DDTL at SOFR+225bp (CoreWeave, Mar-26); Lambda's $500mn pure GPU-residual loan (Lambda, Apr-24) marks the risky end. Early private-credit spread alpha is being competed away by public markets.

Software ARR is direct lending's home turf (CDLI 10.4% asset-level income (Cliffwater, Mar-26)); AI labs remain PE/growth-only — leverage is pushed into compute vehicles (OpenAI ~$4bn RCF undrawn (OpenAI, Oct-24); xAI SPV up to $12.5bn, GPU-secured (Bloomberg, Oct-25)), a signal that lab-level cash flow is not yet lendable.

deep (several deals of the same nature); ◐ some (isolated deals); – structurally absent (ruled out by the business model; Junson estimate). EPC — the shallowest row — is omitted: reach it via equipment order books and development-loan demand. Colo PE is classified under infra equity (no double count). Condensed from Exhibit 8 of the full report.

End-demand shortfall (master risk): capex is deployed years ahead of application revenue; stress travels up the payment chain in reverse — first casualties are weak-counterparty take-or-pay contracts and GPU residuals, the two collateral types anchoring this cycle's credit.
2028 oversupply flip: sanctioned capacity lands 2027–28 just as double-ordering unwinds — turbines, transformers and halls can flip together (mid-2010s turbine bust / 2001 fibre glut pattern).
Circular financing unwind: vendor capital inside customer SPVs means part of reported demand is supplier-funded; the markdown would concentrate in GPU-backed paper.

Rates, duration & the refi wall: Hyperion's 23.6-yr duration at one end; neocloud debt maturing 2027–28, years before its contracts and assets, at the other — a wall meeting wider spreads is the classic failure mode.
Counterparty concentration: chain cash flows funnel through <10 names (NVIDIA, four hyperscalers, a handful of labs); cross-sub-sector diversification is partly illusory.

blocks.html: 6. Fund Evaluation: three types, five questions
blocks.text: 6. Fund Evaluation: three types, five questions

blocks.html: Type A — pure DC / AI-infra thematic equity (fails on sector beta). Type B — diversified infra / real-asset funds with DC as one exposure among several (fails position-by-position: look-through matters more than the label). Type C — AI / digital thematic growth equity around the chain (fails like growth equity). Across all three: is cash yield produced by contracted rent and PPAs, or manufactured by structuring? Test the waterfall, not the target. Five diligence questions: ① actual chain position, not the marketing label; ② what the equity earns — development spread vs growth; ③ bottleneck owner or hostage (are slots and pre-leases locked); ④ where the cash yield comes from, benchmarked to the anchors in §3; ⑤ which downside rows apply — the 2028 flip and counterparty concentration apply to nearly every fund in this universe.

items: Type A (AIP): vintage concentration — a US$30bn fund deploying into 2027–28 completions is a single-vintage bet on the flip’s timing; tenant credit mix and pre-leasing on the pipeline; exit cap-rate assumptions vs today’s compressed levels; sponsor conflicts where strategic partners are simultaneously investors, suppliers and tenants; fees on committed vs invested capital.

Type B (PG NGI, OREF VI): position-by-position look-through of NAV and pipeline; evergreen liquidity terms vs asset illiquidity and NAV-based entry pricing; PPA counterparty, tenor and renegotiation triggers — stranded-generation risk where deposits precede signed demand; for net-lease books, tenant tiering (the 7.0–11.0% cap-rate spread is the market pricing it), lease–debt tenor matching, and whether pref equity is income or deferred development risk.

Type C (Digital Alpha): what the cash yield legally is (coupon / revenue share / return of capital) and whether coverage is demonstrated; ~50% single-partner sourcing is an origination risk as well as an edge; whether “unleveraged” holds at the structure level, not just the deal level; which chain counterparties stand behind portfolio-company revenue.

blocks.html: How this feeds our process: ① map the watch items of the report’s Exhibit 12 into the quarterly monitoring sheet for any fund with concentrated sub-sector exposure; ② stress portfolios on the two scenarios this report implies — a 2028 supply flip and a single anchor-counterparty event — rather than on generic spread widening; ③ prefer collateral whose value rests on contract quality over residual-value assumptions: the risks in §5 erode the second faster than the first. As manager decks arrive, each fund gets one row in the comparison log and one completed scorecard (report Exhibits 13–14), with its downside mapping feeding the monitoring sheet.
